verdict: Caution: lend selectively to GI-certified, export-linked Pashmina/Kani/Sozni units with clean certification and verified buyer orders; avoid undifferentiated grey-market shawl traders and power-intensive units until J&K demand signals recover.
title: Srinagar Woollen & Shawl Textiles: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Srinagar shawl unit buys raw Pashmina/wool, converts it through spinning, weaving and Sozni/Kani hand embroidery, and sells to wholesalers, exporters and tourists.** Cash comes in on delivery to bulk buyers and export houses, but the embroidery stage is slow and hand-driven, so work-in-progress sits on the floor for weeks. **The value is in the GI tag and the craft, not the yarn** — which is why the PTQCC at CDI Srinagar nearly doubling GI testing capacity for Kashmir Pashmina, Kani and Sozni matters [1]. **Capex is light (looms, embroidery frames); working capital is the real exposure** — ICRA notes fabric-making working capital is driven by inventory holding and receivables [10]. So when a proposal lands, check the inventory-and-receivable days first; if receivables stretch beyond the stated buyer credit terms, ask for the buyer-wise ageing and the export order copies.

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is weak even as the national textile print is strong.** J&K GST collections are -10.6% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, and electricity demand is -0.5% against India +9.5% [D]. **National woollen output is expanding — IIP NIC 13 is +13.1% YoY and +11.9% Apr-to-date [D] — but that is an India number, not a Srinagar number.** On the ground, exports of Kashmiri handicrafts have crossed Rs 1,100 crore with a Rs 2,000-crore target [3][2]; treat the target as aspiration, not a booked order. **Peer results are mixed and mostly not Kashmir-specific:** Prakash Woollen's Q1FY27 profit came only from a Rs 648.05 lakh NHAI land compensation, with an operating loss of Rs 218.11 lakh [4][5]; Iris Clothings grew total income 40.3% YoY to Rs 62.22 crore at a 15.2% EBITDA margin [6]; Arvind's Q2 net profit rose 44% to Rs 148 crore [7]. **Sources say little about Srinagar city itself, so lean on first principles plus these peers.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue the GI-certified, export-linked borrower:** units that can show PTQCC test certificates [1], a named export buyer, and a design-led product mix. **Pursue the small artisan aggregator** who supplies organised exporters and can show repeat buyer orders. **Avoid the undifferentiated grey-market shawl trader** with no certification, no named buyer and inventory that cannot be aged. **Avoid power-intensive processing units** until the J&K electricity-demand signal turns [D].

## How to grow safely
**Structure as cash credit against a drawing power built on certified stock and verified receivables, with a term loan only for loom/frame capex.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, monthly GST returns, and quarterly buyer-wise sales. **Covenant on receivable days and inventory turns; if either slips beyond the sanctioned limit, freeze the drawing power.** Rating methodology flags that weaving is fixed- and working-capital intensive and that low leverage protects through downturns [8][11] — so cap total debt at a level the unit can service from operating cash, not from one-off items like land compensation [4].

## Early-warning signs
- **GST turnover falling month-on-month while stock rises** — ask for the buyer-wise sales register and re-assess drawing power.
- **Receivable days stretching past the stated buyer terms** — ask for export order copies and buyer confirmation.
- **GI certificate lapses or testing rejections at PTQCC** — suspend fresh disbursement until re-certification [1].
- **Electricity bill arrears or load reduction** — check the latest bill and meter reading; J&K demand is already -0.5% [D].
- **Reliance on non-operating income to show profit** — strip it out and test operating cash flow [4].
